triage.name: Pink Eye
triage.reason: Common red-eye complaint with a differential (viral, bacterial, allergic, keratitis) reachable by history, exam and point-of-care testing.

demographics: Very common in children and young adults, especially in daycare and school settings
Allergic conjunctivitis is more common in people with a personal or family history of atopy
Bacterial conjunctivitis is more common in children than adults

risk_factors.text: Close contact with someone who has infectious conjunctivitis
Personal or family history of atopy (allergic rhinitis, asthma, eczema)
Use of shared towels, pillowcases, or eye makeup

exposures: Sick contacts with red or pink eyes
Pollen, dust mites, animal dander, molds

chief_complaints.text: My eye is red and pink
My eye is itchy and watery
My eye is stuck shut in the morning
My eye feels gritty and burning

hpi.onset: Gradual over 1–2 days; viral and bacterial often start in one eye and spread to the other within a few days
hpi.duration: Usually 1–2 weeks for viral; bacterial may improve within 2–5 days with treatment; allergic lasts as long as allergen exposure
hpi.progression: Redness and discharge worsen over the first few days, then gradually improve; viral may start in one eye and spread to the other
hpi.location: One or both eyes; often bilateral but can be asymmetric
hpi.quality: Redness, irritation, gritty or burning sensation, itching (especially allergic), watery or thick discharge
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; usually not severe pain
hpi.timing: Constant while awake; discharge may accumulate overnight and cause morning sticking

associated_symptoms.text: Recent or current upper respiratory symptoms

pertinent_negatives: Unilateral red eye with contact lens wear
History of recurrent herpes simplex keratitis
Foreign body sensation that persists after blinking

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children may not describe itching or grittiness; they present with eye rubbing, irritability, and parents noticing redness or discharge.
missing_classic_features: Clear description of itching or foreign body sensation

atypical.how_it_differs: May have more severe symptoms and higher risk of complications; bacterial conjunctivitis can be more serious and may be associated with dry eye or blepharitis.
Can develop severe or atypical infections, including fungal or herpes simplex, with more pain and corneal involvement.

Presentation is similar, but treatment options may be limited; gonococcal and chlamydial conjunctivitis should be considered if there is a history of sexually transmitted infection or neonatal exposure.

general.mild: Comfortable, alert, no distress; eye redness noted but patient interacts normally
general.moderate: Mild discomfort, occasionally rubs the eye, otherwise well-appearing
general.severe: Uncomfortable, photophobic, keeps the affected eye closed or shaded
general.critical: Ill-appearing, toxic, or systemically unwell; consider a sight-threatening or systemic cause rather than simple conjunctivitis

findings.maneuver: Inspect the bulbar and palpebral conjunctiva in natural light
findings.finding: Diffuse conjunctival redness that is most prominent peripherally and fades toward the limbus

findings.maneuver: Inspect the eyelid margins and lower fornix for discharge
findings.finding: Watery or mucoid discharge (viral or allergic) or thick purulent discharge (bacterial)
Mild eyelid swelling or crusting along the lashes

findings.maneuver: Evert the lower eyelid and inspect the palpebral conjunctiva
findings.finding: Small lymphoid follicles on the palpebral conjunctiva, favoring viral or chlamydial cause

findings.maneuver: Evert the upper eyelid and inspect the palpebral conjunctiva
findings.finding: Papillary reaction with central vessels, favoring allergic or bacterial cause

findings.maneuver: Palpate the preauricular and submandibular lymph nodes
findings.finding: Tender preauricular lymph node, more typical of viral conjunctivitis

findings.maneuver: Check pupil size, symmetry, and reactivity to light
findings.finding: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light without afferent pupillary defect

findings.maneuver: Check visual acuity with a Snellen chart or age-appropriate method
findings.finding: Visual acuity is normal or at the patient's baseline

findings.maneuver: Inspect the perilimbal region with a light
findings.finding: No ciliary flush or deep perilimbal injection

findings.maneuver: Inspect the cornea with a light; perform fluorescein staining if available
findings.finding: Cornea is clear without opacity, ulcer, or fluorescein uptake

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the orbits from above and below
findings.finding: No proptosis, periorbital swelling, or restricted extraocular movements

findings.maneuver: Evert the eyelids and inspect the fornices and conjunctival sac
findings.finding: No foreign body, no retained contact lens, no corneal abrasion

initial.why: Establishes a baseline and screens for vision loss, which argues against simple conjunctivitis

initial.test: Fluorescein staining with slit-lamp or blue light examination
initial.why: Detects corneal epithelial defects or dendritic ulcers suggesting keratitis or herpes simplex
initial.only_if: eye pain, photophobia, contact lens wear, or decreased vision

initial.why: Identifies influenza when systemic symptoms are present and antiviral therapy is considered
initial.only_if: fever, myalgias, or respiratory symptoms during influenza season

supporting.test: Conjunctival swab for bacterial culture and Gram stain
supporting.why: Identifies the organism in severe, recurrent, or treatment-resistant bacterial conjunctivitis
supporting.only_if: severe purulent discharge, suspected gonococcal or chlamydial infection, or failure of empiric antibiotics

supporting.test: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for herpes simplex virus and adenovirus
supporting.why: Confirms viral cause when herpes keratitis or an adenoviral outbreak is suspected
supporting.only_if: dendritic corneal lesions, severe pain, or known outbreak setting

supporting.test: Chlamydia trachomatis nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT)
supporting.why: Detects chlamydial conjunctivitis in chronic or recurrent cases with genital or neonatal exposure
supporting.only_if: chronic follicular conjunctivitis, sexually transmitted infection risk, or neonatal exposure

not_indicated.why: Uncomplicated conjunctivitis is a localized condition; blood counts do not change management
No role in diagnosing or managing simple conjunctivitis
No role in diagnosing or managing simple conjunctivitis
Not relevant to eye redness or discharge
Not relevant to eye redness or discharge
Not indicated for conjunctivitis; reserved for suspected orbital cellulitis or abscess
not_indicated.only_if: proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, severe pain, or systemic toxicity

not_indicated.why: Not indicated for conjunctivitis; reserved for suspected orbital or intracranial extension
not_indicated.only_if: suspected orbital cellulitis, abscess, or cavernous sinus thrombosis

not_indicated.why: Not indicated for conjunctivitis; used for suspected retinal or vitreous pathology

decision_points: Check visual acuity and fluorescein staining before diagnosing simple conjunctivitis; pain, photophobia, or vision loss suggest keratitis, uveitis, or acute angle-closure glaucoma
Remove contact lenses and consider corneal culture in contact lens wearers with a red eye
Consider gonococcal or chlamydial conjunctivitis in sexually active patients or neonates with severe purulent discharge
Refer urgently to ophthalmology for suspected herpes simplex keratitis, corneal ulcer, or sight-threatening disease

differential.name: Herpes simplex keratitis
differential.why_considered: Red, watery, irritated eye that can look like viral conjunctivitis, especially with a red eye and tearing
differential.trigger: Eye pain out of proportion to findings, photophobia, decreased vision, or a branching (dendritic) corneal lesion on fluorescein staining

history: Unilateral eye pain, often more severe than simple conjunctivitis
Prior episodes of cold sores or herpes keratitis
Recent topical steroid use for a red eye
exam: Decreased visual acuity in the affected eye
Dendritic or geographic corneal ulcer on fluorescein staining
labs: HSV PCR from a conjunctival or corneal swab when the diagnosis is uncertain

differential.name: Bacterial keratitis (corneal ulcer)
differential.why_considered: Red, painful, discharging eye, particularly in contact lens wearers, that can be mistaken for bacterial conjunctivitis
differential.trigger: Contact lens wear with a red, painful eye, photophobia, or a corneal opacity/fluorescein uptake

history: Contact lens wear, especially overnight or with poor hygiene
Foreign body sensation that persists after blinking
exam: Corneal opacity, infiltrate, or fluorescein uptake
labs: Corneal scraping for Gram stain and culture when an ulcer is present

differential.name: Acute angle-closure glaucoma
differential.why_considered: Acutely red eye that can be mistaken for conjunctivitis if the patient focuses on redness rather than pain and vision
differential.trigger: Severe unilateral eye pain with headache, nausea or vomiting, halos around lights, and a mid-dilated fixed pupil

history: Sudden severe eye or brow pain
History of hyperopia or prior angle-closure attack
exam: Markedly elevated intraocular pressure on tonometry

differential.name: Anterior uveitis (iritis)
differential.why_considered: Red, painful, photophobic eye that can be mistaken for conjunctivitis when redness is the main complaint
differential.trigger: Deep eye pain, photophobia, and ciliary flush with a relatively quiet discharge

history: Associated autoimmune disease or prior episodes
exam: Cells and flare in the anterior chamber on slit-lamp examination
labs: Testing for underlying systemic disease (for example HLA-B27, ANA) when recurrent or bilateral

differential.name: Orbital or preseptal cellulitis
differential.why_considered: Eyelid swelling and redness with a red eye that can be mistaken for conjunctivitis when swelling is prominent
differential.trigger: Fever, marked eyelid swelling, proptosis, painful or restricted eye movements, or systemic toxicity

exam: Decreased visual acuity in orbital involvement
labs: CBC with differential and blood cultures when systemic infection is suspected
imaging: CT orbits with contrast showing orbital fat stranding, abscess, or sinusitis

differential.name: Allergic conjunctivitis
differential.why_considered: Bilateral red, itchy, watery eyes that are frequently confused with infectious conjunctivitis

history: Personal or family history of atopy (allergic rhinitis, asthma, eczema)
exam: Papillary reaction on the palpebral conjunctiva
Cobblestone papillae under the upper lid in chronic cases

differential.name: Dry eye syndrome
differential.why_considered: Chronic red, gritty, burning eyes that can resemble mild conjunctivitis

history: Chronic, bilateral gritty or burning sensation
Worse with screen use, wind, or dry environments
Older age or use of drying medications
exam: Reduced tear film or tear break-up time

differential.name: Subconjunctival hemorrhage
differential.why_considered: Bright red eye that can alarm patients and be mistaken for conjunctivitis

history: Sudden onset of a red patch, often noticed on waking
Possible preceding cough, sneeze, or straining
May be on an antiplatelet or anticoagulant
exam: Well-demarcated bright red patch under the conjunctiva
labs: Coagulation studies or platelet count only if bleeding is recurrent or unexplained

severity.mild: Mild redness and watery or mucoid discharge, no pain, normal vision, no photophobia; self-limited and often managed with supportive care
severity.moderate: More prominent redness, thick purulent discharge, eyelid swelling or crusting, mild discomfort; bacterial cases may warrant topical antibiotics
severity.severe: Marked redness and discharge with significant pain, photophobia, or decreased vision; consider keratitis, uveitis, or other sight-threatening causes rather than simple conjunctivitis
severity.critical: Not applicable; simple conjunctivitis is not life-threatening, but systemic toxicity, proptosis, or ophthalmoplegia should prompt evaluation for orbital cellulitis or another serious process

red_flags.finding: Severe eye pain or pain out of proportion to findings
red_flags.meaning: Suggests keratitis, corneal ulcer, uveitis, or acute angle-closure glaucoma rather than simple conjunctivitis
Suggests corneal, intraocular, or optic nerve involvement and requires urgent ophthalmology evaluation
Suggests corneal or intraocular inflammation such as keratitis or uveitis

red_flags.finding: Contact lens wear with a red, painful eye
red_flags.meaning: Consider bacterial or acanthamoeba keratitis; remove lenses and evaluate urgently

red_flags.finding: Proptosis, painful or restricted eye movements, or marked periorbital swelling
red_flags.meaning: Suggests orbital cellulitis or abscess, which is sight-threatening and may spread intracranially
Suggests a systemic infection such as orbital cellulitis, gonococcal infection, or another serious cause

red_flags.finding: Severe purulent discharge with rapid onset in a neonate or sexually active patient
red_flags.meaning: Suggests gonococcal conjunctivitis, which can cause corneal perforation and requires urgent treatment

red_flags.finding: Dendritic corneal lesion on fluorescein staining
red_flags.meaning: Suggests herpes simplex keratitis; avoid topical steroids and refer urgently

complications.name: Scarring and symblepharon (from severe or recurrent inflammation)

special_populations.differences: Very common in daycare and school settings; young children may not describe itching or grittiness and present with eye rubbing, irritability, and parental report of redness or discharge. Bacterial conjunctivitis is more common in children than adults.

Neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum) is a distinct concern; consider gonococcal and chlamydial infection from maternal exposure and evaluate urgently, especially with severe purulent discharge.
May have more severe symptoms and higher risk of complications; bacterial conjunctivitis can be more serious and is often associated with dry eye or blepharitis.
Can develop severe or atypical infections, including fungal or herpes simplex, with more pain and corneal involvement; lower threshold for ophthalmology referral.
Presentation is similar, but treatment options may be limited; consider gonococcal and chlamydial conjunctivitis if there is a history of sexually transmitted infection or neonatal exposure.

key_questions.question: When did the redness start, and did it begin in one eye or both?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over 1–2 days, often starting in one eye and spreading to the other within a few days; sudden bilateral onset after allergen exposure suggests allergic cause

key_questions.question: Is the eye itchy, or does it burn and feel gritty?
key_questions.looking_for: Prominent itching favors allergic conjunctivitis; burning or gritty sensation favors viral or bacterial

key_questions.question: What does the discharge look like — watery, stringy, or thick and pus-like?
key_questions.looking_for: Watery or mucoid discharge suggests viral or allergic; thick purulent discharge suggests bacterial

key_questions.question: Is your eye stuck shut in the morning?
key_questions.looking_for: Morning sticking or crusting is common in bacterial and viral conjunctivitis

key_questions.question: Do you have any eye pain, sensitivity to light, or change in your vision?
key_questions.looking_for: Severe pain, photophobia, or decreased vision argues against simple conjunctivitis and suggests keratitis, uveitis, or acute angle-closure glaucoma

key_questions.question: Do you wear contact lenses, and if so, do you sleep in them or clean them as directed?
key_questions.looking_for: Contact lens wear with a red, painful eye raises concern for bacterial or acanthamoeba keratitis

key_questions.question: Have you had a recent cold, sore throat, or runny nose?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent upper respiratory infection supports viral conjunctivitis

key_questions.question: Has anyone around you had red or pink eyes recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Sick contacts with conjunctivitis support an infectious cause

key_questions.question: Do you have a history of allergies, hay fever, asthma, or eczema?
key_questions.looking_for: Personal or family history of atopy supports allergic conjunctivitis

key_questions.question: Does the redness come and go with seasons, or after being around pets, dust, or pollen?
key_questions.looking_for: Seasonal or allergen-related pattern supports allergic conjunctivitis

key_questions.question: Have you used any eye drops, ointments, or new cosmetics recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Contact lens solutions, eye drops, or cosmetics can cause irritant or allergic conjunctivitis

key_questions.question: Have you had any eye surgery or eye trauma recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent surgery or trauma raises concern for a more serious cause and warrants urgent evaluation

key_questions.question: Do you have any genital discharge, sores, or a history of sexually transmitted infections?
key_questions.looking_for: Gonococcal or chlamydial conjunctivitis in sexually active patients or neonates with severe purulent discharge

reasoning_points: Redness of the conjunctiva with watery, mucoid, or purulent discharge and normal visual acuity
Itching favors allergic conjunctivitis; burning or gritty sensation favors viral or bacterial
Recent upper respiratory infection or sick contacts support an infectious cause
Personal or family history of atopy supports allergic conjunctivitis
Absence of severe pain, photophobia, decreased vision, ciliary flush, and corneal opacity argues against keratitis, uveitis, or acute angle-closure glaucoma
Contact lens wear with a red, painful eye raises concern for keratitis and requires urgent evaluation
Conjunctival injection that is most prominent peripherally and fades toward the limbus, with a clear cornea and normal pupils

easy: Child or young adult with bilateral red, itchy, watery eyes after a recent cold
Diffuse conjunctival injection with normal visual acuity and no pain
Clear cornea and no ciliary flush on exam
Sick contact with pink eye at daycare or school
medium: Bacterial conjunctivitis with thick purulent discharge and morning sticking
Allergic conjunctivitis with seasonal itching and a history of atopy
Adult with contact lens wear and a red eye but no pain or vision change
Unilateral redness that spreads to the other eye over a few days
hard: Contact lens wearer with a red, painful eye and a corneal opacity suggesting keratitis
Patient with severe eye pain, photophobia, and halos around lights suggesting acute angle-closure glaucoma
Neonate with severe purulent discharge suggesting gonococcal or chlamydial conjunctivitis
Immunocompromised patient with atypical or severe conjunctival inflammation
Older adult with chronic red, gritty eyes from dry eye syndrome rather than infection
